chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: Early evidence of human settlement in the area of modern Benin can be found in the Atakora mountain chain of north-western Benin. Systematic surveys and excavations have identified caves, rock shelters and open-air sites with lithic industries spanning the Early, Middle and Later Stone Age.
chapters.narrative: Early evidence of human settlement in the area of modern Benin can be found in the Atakora mountain chain of north-western Benin [S1]. Systematic surveys and excavations have identified caves, rock shelters and open-air sites with lithic industries spanning the Early, Middle and Later Stone Age [S1]. These findings indicate human presence in the Atakora mountain chain through multiple periods of the Stone Age [S1]. The provided excerpts focus solely on this archaeological evidence from north-western Benin and therefore reflect a limited perspective on the broader history of settlement in the modern region [S1].

chapters.title: Genetic studies
chapters.summary: A 2015 study by Maarten Larmuseau et al. investigated the paternal genetic landscape of populations along the Bight of Benin, focusing on four groups from present-day Benin: the Fon, Yoruba, Bariba, and Dendi. Using Y-chromosomal markers, the research revealed significant genetic diversity among these populations, reflecting complex historical migrations and interactions.

events.label: 670 BC
events.text: BDArch identified five archaeological phases and three cultural periods prior to Dahomey's rise, with settlement expansion and nucleation occurring from the Yellow Pottery Period (670–540 BC) through the Sodohomé Period (AD 870–1200).
By AD 1000, clear evidence of small-scale iron smelting appears, expanding by AD 1400 to industrial-scale production.

More than thirty sites have been documented across southern Benin, with induced-draft furnaces and extensive slag heaps indicating massive output—estimated at over four million kilograms of iron between AD 1400 and 1600.

chapters.narrative: A 2015 study by Maarten Larmuseau et al. investigated the paternal genetic landscape of populations along the Bight of Benin [S2]. The research focused on four groups from present-day Benin: the Fon, Yoruba, Bariba, and Dendi [S2]. Using Y-chromosomal markers, the study revealed significant genetic diversity among these populations [S2]. This diversity was interpreted as reflecting complex historical migrations and interactions [S2]. The excerpts provided present only genetic evidence and do not include other historical perspectives on these populations [S2]. No further details on specific markers or quantitative results are included in the excerpt [S2]. The available text limits interpretation to the diversity and migration patterns noted above [S2].

chapters.title: Mythic era - 16th and 17th centuries
chapters.summary: The origins of most Gbe polities are poorly understood, but historical sources indicate that throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, these polities vied for dominance over Atlantic commercial routes. This resulted in significant political and economic expansion.

events.text: From the 1560s, African captives labeled "Aradas" were recorded in Peru, and the city appeared on Portuguese charts after 1570.
It is also possible that the dynasty emerged during the collapse of the iron economy on the plateau around 1600, creating opportunities for new elites to redirect trade toward the coast.

The Dutch West India Company acquired around 800 slaves annually from Allada between 1636 and 1647, and by the 1680s, the Slave Coast exported roughly 5,000 captives per year, increasing to 10,000 by the 1710s.
King Wegbaja (ca. 1650–80) used feasting and redistribution to build alliances with local elites.
By 1670, only 17% of captives were sourced by the king himself.
A minor kingdom and a client of Allada for much of the seventeenth century, Hueda entered the documentary record in 1671 with the establishment of a French trading lodge in Savi, its royal capital.
The English Royal African Company relocated its base to Savi in 1682, leaving the Dutch as the sole European power at Offra.
King Haffon (r. 1708–33) tried to centralize control by restricting access to trade wealth, provoking opposition.
Succession disputes, including Hussar's attempted usurpation of King Soso (1717–24), and revolts in key towns like Offra, destabilized the kingdom.
These internal divisions ultimately enabled Dahomey to conquer Hueda in 1727.

chapters.narrative: The origins of most Gbe polities are poorly understood, but historical sources indicate that throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries these polities vied for dominance over Atlantic commercial routes, resulting in significant political and economic expansion [S3]. From the 1560s African captives labeled "Aradas" were recorded in Peru, and the city appeared on Portuguese charts after 1570 [S3]. It is also possible that the dynasty emerged during the collapse of the iron economy on the plateau around 1600 [S3]. The excerpts reflect a perspective reliant on European documentary and commercial records, as Hueda entered the documentary record in 1671 with the establishment of a French trading lodge in Savi [S3], and the English Royal African Company relocated its base to Savi in 1682 [S3].

chapters.title: Colonial Benin (formerly, Republic of Dahomey)
chapters.summary: Dahomey was a French colony of and a part of French West Africa from 1904 to 1959. Under the French, a port was constructed at Cotonou, and railroads were built.

events.text: Dahomey was a French colony of and a part of French West Africa from 1904 to 1959.
On December 4, 1958, it became the Republic of Dahomey.
Between 1960 and 1972, a succession of military coups brought about many changes of government.
By 1975 the Republic of Dahomey changed its name to the People's Republic of Benin.
President Kérékou was barred from running under the 1990 constitution due to term and age limitations.

The success of a party formed by supporters of ex-president Kérékou, who had officially retired from active politics, allowed him to stand successfully at both the 1996 and 2001 presidential elections.
Nicephore Soglo's Renaissance du Benin (RB) party won the new vote, paving the way for the former president to be elected Mayor of Cotonou by the new city council in February 2002.
President Yayi was inaugurated on April 6, 2006.
In March 2011,  President Boni Yayi was re-elected with 53.13 percent of vote in the first-round of the election.
In October 2015, Benin's former President Mathieu Kerekou, who ruled the country a total of 28 years during his two spells as president (1972-1991 and 1996–2006), died at the age of 82.

chapters.narrative: Dahomey was a French colony and part of French West Africa from 1904 to 1959 [S4]. Under the French, a port was constructed at Cotonou and railroads were built [S4]. On December 4, 1958, it became the Republic of Dahomey [S4]. Between 1960 and 1972, a succession of military coups brought about many changes of government [S4]. By 1975 the Republic of Dahomey changed its name to the People's Republic of Benin [S4]. The available excerpts provided reflect a concise, externally framed chronological overview and do not include Beninese perspectives on colonial or post-colonial experience [S4].
